candidates.attacker_control: The candidate raw password passed to BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches(CharSequence, String) is fully attacker-controlled on every authentication attempt (e.g. login form / Basic auth / DaoAuthenticationProvider). The attacker does not need to modify the stored hash; they only need a credential string whose first 72 UTF-8 bytes equal those of the victim's password.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The 72-byte limit is intrinsic to bcrypt itself (the Blowfish key schedule can only consume 72 key bytes; streamtowords cycles the array), so this is not a memory-safety or parsing bug, and short passwords are unaffected. I verified that upstream-equivalent code elsewhere uses constant-time comparison (MessageDigest.isEqual) and that no other layer (DelegatingPasswordEncoder/PasswordEncoderFactories) adds a length check, so there is no compensating control inside the snapshot. Exploitability therefore depends on the application's password policy (long passwords) and prefix knowledge; I could not verify runtime behavior, tests, or whether a downstream fix exists, since no build/test execution was permitted.
candidates.impact: Authentication with a password that is not the stored one (bypass of the password check) for accounts whose password exceeds 72 bytes, as long as the first 72 bytes are known; credential rotation that changes only the part of the password after the 72nd byte leaves old credentials valid; hashes of distinct long passwords collide, giving users false assurance about the strength/length of long passphrases.
candidates.prerequisites: The application stores BCrypt hashes produced from passwords longer than 72 bytes (encode() accepts them silently), and an attacker can submit a candidate whose first 72 bytes match (e.g. a long shared passphrase/prefix where only the tail was intended to be secret, or a leaked password prefix). Where passwords are shorter than 72 bytes, the issue does not arise.
candidates.root_cause: The Blowfish key schedule consumes exactly 18 32-bit words (72 bytes) of the password: BCrypt.key() iterates i < this.P.length (=18) calling streamtoword() (BCrypt.java:416-429) and BCrypt.ekskey() does the same (BCrypt.java:452-464); streamtowords() advances modulo data.length (BCrypt.java:366-373), so only password bytes 0-71 can ever influence the state. Neither the public hashpw/checkpw entry points (BCrypt.java:588-604, 762-776) nor BCryptPasswordEncoder.encode/matches (BCryptPasswordEncoder.java:105-111, 121-134) check rawPassword/encoded length, warn, or reject inputs longer than 72 bytes; matches() simply recomputes the hash of the candidate and compares it (line 133). The hash of an over-length password is therefore a hash of its 72-byte prefix, and any other string with the same 72-byte prefix yields the identical hash.
candidates.title: BCryptPasswordEncoder/BCrypt silently ignore password bytes after the 72nd, so distinct long passwords compare as equal
candidates.trace: BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches (BCryptPasswordEncoder.java:121) -> BCrypt.checkpw(String, String) (BCrypt.java:762-765) -> hashpwforcheck -> hashpw(byte[], String, true) (BCrypt.java:606-656) -> crypt_raw -> ekskey/key (BCrypt.java:452-464, 416-429) -> streamtowords (BCrypt.java:360-378) reading only 18*4 = 72 password bytes; the resulting digest is compared with MessageDigest.isEqual (BCrypt.java:778-780), so a candidate differing only after byte 72 compares equal.
candidates.unverified: Runtime confirmation that matches() returns true for two distinct over-72-byte inputs was not executed; it is inferred from the key-schedule arithmetic (P.length = 18 words = 72 bytes) and the absence of length checks. Severity in a given deployment depends on password-length policy and attacker knowledge of the 72-byte prefix. I also could not inspect any test suite (crypto tests are absent from this snapshot) or upstream patch content.
candidates.weakness_type: Silent truncation of credential input during password verification (CWE-522 Insufficiently Protected Credentials / improper input-length handling)

coverage_summary: Source scope reports 2,258 model-visible files (source_root_files = model_visible_files), no binary/sensitive-path exclusions, and the P1 index covers 2,225 files (1,969 Java files parsed with 0 parse errors; 36 files omitted; 33 source files absent from the index; control-flow and data-flow analyses are 'not_implemented', call/inheritance edges are syntactic candidates only). I inspected in depth: crypto/bcrypt (BCrypt.java, BCryptPasswordEncoder.java), crypto password encoders (Pbkdf2/Delegating), core authorization and method-security interceptors, web CSRF/redirect/OTT/WebAuthn handlers, config OAuth2/OIDC back-channel logout and one-time-token configuration, and oauth2-jose issuer validation. The remaining majority of the ~1,969 Java files (SAML2, OAuth2 client/server flows, reactive web, LDAP/CAS, ACL, RSocket, Kotlin DSL, buildSrc) were not exhaustively read; coverage statements here refer only to the areas actually inspected.
limitations: No code execution, tests, builds, or scanners were run; all conclusions are static and runtime behavior (including the BCrypt collision in a real login flow) is inferred, not confirmed.
The snapshot contains no BCrypt/unit test suite, so intended behavior could not be cross-checked against tests.

The P1 index provides syntax-level navigation only (no data flow, no semantic resolution, 36 omitted files, 33 source files missing from the index), so reachability and complete input flow were established by manual source reading, not by the index.
Large portions of the repository (SAML2, OAuth2 authorization/resource server, reactive stack, ACL/JDBC, config DSL, buildSrc) were only sampled; a defect there would not have been found.
I could not compare against released 6.4.4 artifacts or repository history (not available in this run), so the root cause is described from the snapshot alone.

rejected_leads.reason: Verified benign: OAuth2TokenValidatorResult.failure(Collection) returns the success (NO_ERRORS) instance when the collection is empty (oauth2/oauth2-core/.../OAuth2TokenValidatorResult.java:82-84), so the result correctly reflects the accumulated errors.

rejected_leads.lead: Webauthn4JRelyingPartyOperations uses WebAuthnManager.createNonStrictWebAuthnManager(), leaves tokenBindingId as null, and dereferences credentialRecord without a null check
rejected_leads.reason: The manager choice and token-binding FIXME are explicit upstream design/defaults (Webauthn4JRelyingPartyOperations.java:99, 248-250, 371-374); no source evidence of a signature/challenge/origin bypass. The missing null check would produce an exception, not an authorization bypass.

The targetUrlParameter/useReferer behavior is opt-in and documented as requiring the application to prevent malicious values (AbstractAuthenticationTargetUrlRequestHandler.java:44-55); the default path uses a configured default URL, so there is no unconditional defect.
Tokens are UUIDv4-based, removed on consume, and expire after 5 minutes (InMemoryOneTimeTokenService.java:43-61); no weakness found in the inspected code.

AuthorityAuthorizationManager uses exact Set containment of granted authorities after role-hierarchy expansion (AuthorityAuthorizationManager.java:79-122, AuthoritiesAuthorizationManager.java:64-75); no case-insensitivity or null-authentication bypass found in the sampled code.

summary: Reviewed the spring-security 6.4.4-SNAPSHOT source tree (2,258 model-visible files, 1,969 Java files parsed by the P1 syntax index) with emphasis on security-critical code paths: crypto/password encoders, core authorization managers and method-security interceptors, servlet web filters (CSRF, redirects, OTT, WebAuthn), OAuth2/OIDC client and JOSE validation. The most concrete, source-evidenced weakness is in the BCrypt implementation: verification silently discards every password byte after the 72nd, and no layer (BCrypt.checkpw or BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches/encode) validates or rejects over-length input, so two different raw passwords that share the first 72 UTF-8 bytes produce the same hash and matches() returns true for the wrong password. All other candidate leads I checked were rejected after verifying the surrounding source. This is a static review only; no code, tests, or scanners were executed.
